articles.title: The Empire Has No Borders
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: For well over a century, Americans have fiercely debated U.S. immigration policy: its merits, flaws, limits, and implications. In recent decades, it has become a central question in electoral and identity politics, largely responsible for the current state of political discourse. Conservatives have long argued that the nation has “lost control” of its borders and frequently decry what they deem as “open borders.” On the other hand, liberals lament what they perceive as a dysfunctional bureaucracy incapable of reconciling humanitarian obligations with the realities of a globalized economic order. Even critics of mass deportation and anti-immigrant dehumanization campaigns begin from the premise that the system has failed to accomplish what it was designed to do . In reality, the opposite is true. Unauthorized migration is not evidence of a broken immigration system; it is one of its defining features. Undocumented migration has persisted despite massive and sustained investment in walls, surveillance, detention, deportation, and legislation designed to stem the flow of “illegal” immigration and strip migrants of access to even the few basic social safety nets that remain after decades of austerity. These policies tell us less about the state’s inability to enforce immigration laws than about their real purpose. For socialists to effectively respond to this system, we must first engage in a systemic re-examination of what immigration policy does, its origins, and its implications. The dominant narrative assumes that the state’s role is primarily to stop the flow of “illegal” immigration. Conservatives and liberals largely disagree only about the degree and the mechanisms that should be employed: Should enforcement be harsher or more permissive? Should legal immigration be expanded or reduced? Should asylum be more accessible or further restricted? These are important questions, but they obscure a more fundamental reality: migration has never been something the United States has tried to eliminate. It is instead something that the U.S. and global economies necessarily produce, demand, and manage. The roots of mass (unauthorized) migration lie in the nation’s history of capitalist development, globalization, and imperialism dating back to the nineteenth century—with implications that remain woefully unexamined, let alone resolved. Undocumented workers occupy a unique position within American capitalism. They harvest crops, process meat, clean hotels, build infrastructure, staff restaurants, care for children and the elderly, and perform essential labor that keeps the economy functioning, consumer prices low, and capital flows stable and predictable. When labor shortages arise, these workers are welcomed. But when economic downturns and crises arise, they are blamed for conditions they neither created nor control. They are, as one journalist put it, “essential but unwanted.” From this perspective, immigration enforcement is less a failed attempt at exclusion and more a remarkably successful regime for governing and disciplining labor. We need not imagine some vast, secret conspiracy among employers, politicians, and border agents. This entire process plays out—and has always played out—in broad daylight. Nor does it require ignoring the competing interests involved: employers have always sought unfettered access to cheap, disposable labor; enforcement agencies have demanded (and received) ever-ballooning budgets and terrifying levels of plenary power; politicians have exploited economic and cultural anxieties by treating migrants as scapegoats in order to win elections without addressing structural inequalities and the material conditions of their constituents. Socialists and labor unions have oscillated between exclusion and solidarity. The system that emerges from these tensions nevertheless coalesces and capitulates to capitalist logic, even if immigration policy was never fully planned or perfectly coherent. At first glance, this logic may appear contradictory. If American employers depend so heavily on immigrant labor, why does the government deploy such a robust immigration enforcement regime and spend billions trying to stop it? The question is reasonable, but embedded in it is the assumption that immigration enforcement exists to shut down unsanctioned migration, to eliminate it altogether. In reality, enforcement serves to regulate flows and to guarantee the presence of a useful but precarious workforce—always available to employers but invariably vulnerable to detention, deportation, and exclusion. This vulnerability suppresses workers’ collective bargaining power while allowing politicians to claim that they are securing the border and preventing some imagined “invasion.” The result is not that migration stops, but that it is carefully managed: providing enough workers to satisfy labor demand and at the same time, enough enforcement to preserve the illusion of border control and the distinction between deserving citizens and “illegal” workers whose status and presence always remains conditional. The case of Mexico The U.S.-Mexico border itself is a product of conquest, settler colonialism, and imperial expansion. The “line” separating the United States and Mexico did not emerge from some natural geographic feature, or for that matter, from differing cultures or economies. It was drawn and imposed through war. After its independence, the United States grew rapidly and ferociously at the expense of Black, indigenous, and immigrant populations. By the end of the 19 th century, the nation had expanded across the continent, eventually stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The budding American empire then looked south to Mexico. After Mexico’s independence, Texas in particular posed a dilemma for the new nation: promising but underdeveloped land and few Mexicans to govern it or protect it from constant Indigenous raids, which were common at the time. The solution was to recruit Americans to settle, improve, and invest in the region and its land. Mexican authorities quickly became resentful of its American migrants: hundreds, then thousands of Americans heeded the call but rejected Mexican culture, refused to learn Spanish or embrace the predominant religion, or even migrate through legal channels. The irony, in hindsight, is breathtaking. In time, these arrivals, along with many of the Mexican citizens living there, developed their own sense of identity and in 1836, fought for independence from Mexico. That came to fruition when James K. Polk signed a joint resolution drafted and passed by Congress, officially admitting Texas to the union as its 28 th state in 1845. Tensions remained, as Mexico continued to claim Texas as part of its legitimate territory. Even when it reluctantly relinquished claims to the state, disagreements regarding the precise boundary of the new border lingered—with the U.S. claiming that Texas extended south to the Rio Grande and Mexico holding claims to the Nueces River further north. On April 25, 1846, Mexican soldiers engaged an American military patrol, killing eleven soldiers, wounding six, and capturing some fifty others. This was the justification Polk needed for an all-out assault, declaring that Mexico had “invaded our territory and shed American blood upon the American soil.” Congress declared war on May 13, 1846. Using its riches and overwhelming military might, the United States made quick work of the fragile Mexican army. In just two years, the assault left 25,000 Mexicans dead (some 13,000 Americans died during the war) and the Mexican military and political establishment humiliated. In exchange for peace and $15 million, Mexico ceded not only claims to Texas but all of what is now California, Nevada, and Utah, as well as large portions of current-day Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado, as well as smaller portions of Wyoming, Kansas, and Oklahoma. Notably and critically, it also absorbed some 50,000-100,000 people who lived in those territories. For the United States, it was a windfall: it acquired over half of Mexican territory, which included rich land, natural resources, and economically enticing geography, all while limiting the number of brown people it had to accept into its newly drawn borders since the region remained sparsely populated. The U.S. conquest of northern Mexico redrew the political map of North America, even as it left intact longstanding economic and social relationships. Communities that had long existed as coherent social spaces suddenly found themselves divided by an international boundary. The border moved over people long before people moved across the border. Promised U.S. citizenship, these new Americans remained second-class citizens: their land claims denied, their culture attacked, their language suppressed, and their rights violated. While human mobility was restricted, capital crossed the newly created border with minimal friction. Railroads linked Mexican agricultural regions to American markets, U.S. investors acquired vast holdings in Mexican mining, agriculture, and transportation. The border allowed capital unrestricted mobility while creating artificial divisions of previously Mexican territories and communities. During the regime of Porfirio Diaz (1876-1911), foreign investment in Mexico reached $1.6 billion, a sum overwhelmingly controlled by U.S. interests (much of the rest belonging to Britain and France). The result was that Mexican workers increasingly found their livelihoods shaped by economic forces far removed from their local communities. Industrialization, commercial agriculture, and foreign investment transformed rural life, creating some new opportunities but displacing millions. By the end of the first decade of the twentieth century, Mexico had become a political pressure cooker. Vast wealth lined the pockets of the Diaz regime and foreign investors, even as peasants lost communal land and workers in factories, railroads, and mines faced increasingly dangerous working conditions, the loss of legal protections, and stagnating wages, leading to peasant revolts and ultimately a full-scale civil war. The Mexican Revolution left one million dead and led hundreds of thousands of survivors to flee the country and seek refuge in the United States. Migrants included ordinary workers, intellectuals, and leftist radicals, like the Magón Brothers—Ricardo, Enrique, and Jesús—who lived in exile in the United States, where they organized an international political movement, published the radical newspaper Regeneración , and worked with labor movements on both sides of the border, aiding the revolutionary effort from places like San Antonio, St. Louis, and Los Angeles, even as they faced severe political repression there themselves. After a decade of civil war, Mexican society was fundamentally transformed, replacing the Porfirian regime with a revolutionary state that claimed legitimacy through social reform, nationalism, and inclusion of workers and peasants in political life. Nevertheless, proximity and the entangled political economies of both countries would continue to complicate Mexico’s revolutionary promise for decades, and outmigration remained a central piece of the puzzle, primarily by serving as an “escape valve” for economic refugees, and an opportunity for capitalist exploitation, corruption, and systemic violence. Creating the Border By the 1920s, the U.S. had begun to institutionalize the border apparatus, one recognizable to us today. Nativism was far from new, of course. Earlier waves of nativism had targeted Irish and Chinese immigrants, but by this point, a coalition of eugenicists and anti-communists pushed for broad legal restrictions against foreigners, and after World War I, the U.S. passed a major piece of racist immigration legislation (“Johnson-Reed”) that drastically reduced the flow migrants from Asia as well as southern and eastern Europe. With the exception of the most radical industrial unions, like the IWW, most labor groups sided squarely with restrictionist factions, operating under the assumption that foreign workers diluted wages, weakened labor power, and prevented assimilation of immigrant workers—or worse, imported radical ideologies that would make the movement a target of Red Scare terror. Mexican migration was not, however, initially a major source of concern. Like the rest of the Hemisphere, Mexico was exempted from the 1924 quotas, not out of benevolence, but because agricultural interests relied on their cheap labor, which was largely circular and seasonal and mostly invisible to most Americans. However, attitudes toward Mexican migrants changed rapidly during the Great Depression as jobs became scarce and relief programs strained, making these workers prime political scapegoats. Governments—at both the federal and state/local levels responded by waging a mass “repatriation” campaign that resulted in the expulsion of some one million ethnic Mexicans, a majority of them U.S. citizens. The dynamics of Mexican migration evolved again during and after World War II. As the U.S. entered the fight against the Axis Powers, with over sixteen million men eventually fighting overseas, the home front faced a massive labor shortage, especially in agriculture. The solution was a bilateral agreement known as the Bracero Program, which imported hundreds of thousands, eventually millions of men (the program was not available to women) to work in that sector, along with some others (especially railroads). Alongside the Braceros came larger numbers of undocumented, unsanctioned workers representing roughly twice the number of contracted workers. The program, which was initially slated to end at the conclusion of the war, did not in fact end then. Instead, it was formalized when the Korean War began. In time, those who “saved the crops” became the targets of nativist ire. By the early 1950s, some one million Mexican workers, most of them unsanctioned, were thought to be working in the United States. The nativist panic that ensued, driven by the recession of 1953 and by racist fantasies about the perceived dangers of Mexican men, prompted the government to respond, but it did so in ways that revealed in stark terms the true nature and function of immigration policy. With the backing of restrictionists, white supremacists, and even the leading Mexican American civic groups who viewed Mexican migration as a threat to assimilation and labor organizing, the U.S. launched a mass deportation campaign, dubbed “Operation Wetback.” Officially, the U.S. deported some one million people. But this was starkly different from repatriation in the 1930s: first of all, the entire undertaking was little more than a publicity stunt. As historians Kelly Lyttle Hernández, Ramon Garciá, and others have noted, the vast majority of those expelled were voluntary departures or deportations to border areas where migrants were given a proverbial wink and access to a quick return. Again, illustrating the ways in which migration control served the interests of capital, the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act had made it a felony to smuggle, transport or harbor unauthorized workers, but thanks to pressure and influence from Texas growers, the “Texas Proviso” loophole inserted into the law shielded employers (nationwide, not just in Texas) from prosecution. It allowed authorities and employers to collaborate in remarkably brazen, corrupt ways: many “illegals” were summarily “paroled” and given Bracero permits, sometimes on the spot. Others, officially deported, were recruited again as Braceros almost immediately. The entire operation, in other words, was designed to give employers near-total control of labor flows while selling a vision of law and order to the American public. Family Reconciliation: Myth and Reality The Bracero program finally ended in 1964, after pressure from civil rights leaders, Mexican American intellectuals, and labor organizers who rightly concluded that the use of “semi-slaves” as the leading Mexican American labor organizer Ernesto Galraza called them due to their status as effectively rightless “guest” laborers, made labor organizing impossible. That same year, Congress passed the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1964 (“Hart-Celler” named after its main sponsors, Michigan Senator Philip A. Hart, a Democrat and New York Congressman Emanuel Celler, a Republican). It eliminated the blatantly racist underpinnings of the national origins act of 1924 so as not to embarrass the United States in its alleged crusade for freedom in the Cold War against the Soviet Union. One of its stated goals was family reunification. However, the new immigration regime created massive obstacles for Mexican (and more broadly, Latin American) immigrants, as they now faced limits on legal migration and a tiered “preference” system. Skilled workers and those with immediate relatives found a relatively easy path to legal status, but millions of ordinary workers without family ties to the United States seeking work in the country had to do so illegally. Backlogs grew consistently throughout the decades , even as the number of undocumented people did too. By the 1970s, some one million unsanctioned laborers were thought to be in the country again, and a new nativist wave dominated the political response, in the process further exposing the flaws and contradictions of capitalist logic. The Resistance to capitalist illogic While nativists and restrictionists sought a hardline approach against migration, employers insisted that they were entitled to hire foreign labor, claiming that Americans refused to do the work that immigrants did. Although still taken as gospel among pundits and observers, the cliché that “immigrants do the work Americans won’t do,” was patently false. The reality was that Americans refused to do the work as cheaply and under the same precarious conditions as immigrants. At the same time, left-wing organizers, including many leading Mexican Americans—once fiercely opposed to immigrant labor—were rethinking established assumptions and strategies. Labor activists like Miguel Pendas and Humberto “Bert” Corona, both socialists based in California, argued that playing by capital’s rules could never yield gains for workers. What if, they asked, instead of seeking restriction and criminalization, undocumented workers could be organized? What if the entire logic of border politics was fundamentally flawed and anti-worker? If capital could ignore national boundaries in pursuit of profits, they reasoned, why shouldn’t workers across borders also see themselves as “one people without borders”? Only trans- and international solidarity could alleviate the problems facing the working class. The most radical immigrant rights activists, like the Chicano restauranter and convicted gun runner Mario Cantú suggested that the system as it existed rewarded capital and punished workers on both sides of the border: Mexican authorities could simply push poverty out of sight and out of mind by encouraging its most impoverished populations to migrate north, even as those workers were used to suppress labor gains in the U.S. For Cantú and other revolutionary thinkers, nothing short of armed rebellion in Mexico could solve the problem. Other activists remained more focused on internal and more gradual political solutions, even as they looked abroad for models of transnational solidarity. In Europe, where “irregular” migration had also become a hot-button issue, some of the more militant unions had taken a different approach to migration. Switzerland’s Clothing and Leather Workers Union, France’s General Conference of Labor, and the French Democratic Federation of Labor adopted the then-novel position that migration and its ill effects on workers was the result of “super-exploitation” and argued that immigrants should be approached as “an integral part of the working class” and protected and integrated into the class struggle. The logic of the immigration debate, they contended, had to be flipped on its head: by deliberately taking advantage of the most vulnerable workers—often immigrants—employers found it easier to undermine organizing efforts and to suppress wages and efforts at improved working conditions. Conversely, a united front of workers, foreign and domestic, could produce a meaningful opposition to exploitation and abuse. In the U.S., most labor unions remained unconvinced that embracing the undocumented was prudent. The United Farm Workers Union, led by the now-disgraced Cesar Chavez, continued through the early 1970s to oppose immigrant rights. Under Chavez’s leadership, the union regularly called for raids, deportations, and restrictions—at one point even creating its own (poorly trained, ineffective) border patrol (the so-called “wet line”) to detain and turn over migrants to immigration authorities. Only after intense criticism and pressure from Chicano leaders and radical organizers, did the union shift its position in 1975, with Chavez passively admitting that “mistakes” had been made “in the heat of the struggle.” Its reversal was less a result of altruism and moral reflection than a recognition of the changing realities in the fields. By that time, undocumented workers made up a huge proportion—in some regions a majority—of the workforce. If the union was to represent anyone, it would have to accept that those workers were unsanctioned. Other unions, however, remained recalcitrant. The AFL-CIO had begun to soften its anti-immigrant rhetoric, and signs appeared that change was in the air, as when the federation voted, for the first time in 1980, on whether to adopt a more inclusive posture. Immigrant rights activists, however, lost the vote. George Meany and his associates remained unwilling to reverse course for some time. The AFL-CIO only officially took a more explicitly pro-immigrant stance in the year 2000. The Politics of immigration Through the 1980s, policymakers responded to mass migration by seeking new reforms that attempted to ease the contradictions of the immigration regime without fundamentally restructuring its foundations. It was under Jimmy Carter that the concept of “compressive immigration reform” first took shape. Carter established the Select Commission on Immigration and Refugee Policy in 1978, tapping Ted Hesburgh (then president of the University of Notre Dame and a universally respected figure) to lead it. The commission studied the issue extensively and presented its recommendations in 1981 , suggesting a three-pronged approach to immigration reform: increased enforcement to satisfy restrictionists, the creation of an agricultural guest worker program akin to the Bracero system to appease employers, and amnesty for undocumented people already in the country designed to gain favor with the growing and increasingly pro-immigrant Hispanic lobby. With the bipartisan sponsorship of Alan Simpson, the Republican senator from Wyoming and Romano Mazzoli, the Democratic Congressman from Kentucky, Ronald Reagan endorsed the legislative package. Congress, after several failed attempts, finally passed the law in 1986, with Reagan promising that it would “improve the lives of a class of individuals who now must hide in the shadows, without access to many of the benefits of a free and open society” while also “[increasing] enforcement of the immigration laws.” However much Reagan depicted the law as a grand solution, it did little to resolve the contradictions embedded in liberal capitalist logic. Migration continued, and so did nativist politics. With huge numbers of undocumented workers arriving in California in particular, restrictionists ferociously attacked immigrant workers and families there. A group of restrictionists, led by state assemblyman Dick Mountjoy, former INS commissioner Alan Nelson, former regional director of the INS Harold Ezell, and Orange County accountant Ron Prince, crafted a harsh and punitive ballot initiative, Proposition 187, that sought to deny undocumented people and their families access to social services, including education and healthcare. Few imagined that the law would prevent migration or do anything about the number of immigrants already in the state. Instead, it embraced the logic of the libertarian economist Milton Friendman, who some decades prior had outlined perhaps the most honest assessment of how free market fundamentalists viewed the function of immigration policies and priorities. Asked in 1978 whether he, as a libertarian, supported more open borders, Friedman had replied that “Mexican immigration . . . is a good thing. It’s a good thing for the illegal immigrants. It’s a good thing for the United States. It’s a good thing for the citizens of the country. But it’s only good as long as it’s illegal.” In other words, the economic contributions of immigrants were invaluable, but only if they did not expect anything in return from the society that extracted their labor. Proposition 187 was popular and its proponents wildly successful at the ballot box, with voters supporting it by a two-to-one margin. Organizers quickly mobilized to wage legal battles, and within a few years, the law’s provisions were struck down as unconstitutional due to its brazenly discriminatory, racist cornerstones. But anti-immigrant attacks and the paradoxes of immigration control did not fade away. Neither was it purely a right-wing cause; it was broadly bipartisan. If Prop 187 failed to achieve its draconian goals, immigration control continued by other means, with the full and enthusiastic support of the liberal-Democratic political establishment. Under Bill Clinton, Operation Gatekeeper increased the number of border patrol agents from 4,200 in 1994 to almost 10,000 in 2000 and doubled the border budget from $400 million to $800 between 1993 and 1997 (by 2010, it had reached $7.6 billion). Tighter security in busy (urban) crossing areas funneled migrants toward more dangerous crossing paths, resulting in the deaths of several thousand border crossers over the next several years. At the same time, the United States continued to foster illegal migration through its disastrous imperial foreign policy. “Free trade” initiatives, most notably the North American Free Trade Agreement flooded agricultural Mexico’s markets and displaced Mexican farmers. The lingering effects of military interventions and support for anti-democratic regimes in Central America (among them Guatemala, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Panama) over the previous decades, and the parallel development of what historian Adam Goodman calls a “deportation machine,” led to political instability, mass poverty, and the growth of gang violence in those countries. Naturally, that motivated ordinary Central Americans to seek an escape from these conditions—ironically but revealingly, into the very country that had caused those conditions. The more migrants the United States produced, the more it fed anti-immigrant sentiment at home, and the more the U.S. government responded with harsh restrictions, thus creating and recreating a vicious and inhumane but entirely predictable cycle. And if Prop 187 had failed the constitutional test, its architects played the long game. In fact, there is ample evidence that their goals were far more ideological than legal. By positioning aggrieved Americans as the victims of not only migrant populations but also an unresponsive state, they built a robust nativist machine and movement that demonized immigrants and blamed them for economic and social woes. Ron Prince, who financially ruined himself funding Prop 187, suggested in 1996, while the case was still being heard in federal courts, that the entire episode proved “we were right” and promised to be “the ACLU of the 21 st century.” In this reactionary environment, further exacerbated by the post-9/11 “war on terror” and by liberalism’s failure to offer a compelling economic response to globalization’s disastrous effects on workers, the rise of Donald Trump and his reactionary “Make America Great Again” movement in the twenty-first century was as predictable as it was tragic. In response, immigrant rights activists have continued to wage a courageous fight over the years: in the streets, in courtrooms, and notably, in workplaces. Most labor unions have reversed their historical aversion to organizing undocumented workers: the United Farm Workers Union, though a shell of its former self, often downplays its anti-immigrant history. The now weakened AFL-CIO fully embraces “immigration reform.” And unions representing economic sectors with a high concentration of immigrant workers, like the Service Employees International Union, have taken a decidedly pro-immigrant stance. Still, too often, these groups fall into the trap of framing the immigration system as broken, as a national problem, and as something that can be understood and addressed apart from its bloody imperial history. Mere pro-immigrant rhetoric that insists the system must be “reformed” offers little chance of addressing, let alone countering, the true function of immigration control, which is worker discipline and the dismantling of transnational, multi-ethnic worker solidarity.
