articles.title: The Legal Paths to Hoarding Political and Economic Power
articles.author: Aziz Huq
articles.content: It’s a moment for both hope and hesitation: recent victories in Michigan, Colorado, Minnesota, and New York suggest gathering political momentum on the left. Yet a defeat in Wisconsin and a judge’s temporary stay of New York City’s pied-à-terre tax offer reminders that every movement for social progress breeds its own countervailing reaction. But how does that reaction itself build power? The scaffolding for backlash, as the New York City decision suggests, is often found in the legal system.Steep barriers to court access as well as the formidably technical nature of many legal disputes mean that insiders commonly have the ability not merely to secure the outcomes they want, but also to shape the rules under which notionally fair competition unfolds. This “playing for rules,” rather than for specific results, means that law often offers the inside track for incumbents’ ground-rigging projects.Across seemingly unrelated legal developments, lawyers and judges have been pursuing such projects of late. Each change is leading to a concentration of power in electoral politics and economic power, in ways that insulate insiders. And the effects accumulate: they feed each other, leading to a vicious circle of increasingly obdurate concentrations of power.Until Francesca Hong’s defeat this week, it was possible to write off the central organs of the Democratic Party as wholly incapacitated by debt and internal dysfunction under the leadership of Ken Martin’s hapless Democratic National Committee (DNC). Yet the institutional party has lately gained two tools that give it greater leverage, if not to win general elections then at least to police ideological purity at the primary stage.The first is a newfound power for partisan gerrymandering. This is a gift from our antidemocratic Supreme Court, which has anointed partisan advantage as a justification in mapmaking while dismantling the Voting Rights Act’s protections for minorities. To see the consequences, consider what unfolded earlier this year in California. Responding to Republican gerrymanders in Texas and Florida, Governor Gavin Newsom pushed through a referendum and then a new congressional map. Its lines were drawn by a “veteran Democratic redistricting expert in Sacramento” in “consultation” with the state’s Democratic congressional delegation. In court, the state’s lawyers successfully defended the map on the ground that it protected Democratic insiders’ seats.However justified California’s response to the Texas and Florida gerrymanders may be as a matter of national politics, it illustrates an unexpected effect of the new partisan gerrymandering: It is inevitably incumbent insiders who draw the maps. Just as they can be expected to draw out their opponents across the aisle, so too they can be expected to hobble challengers from the margin. Gerrymandering does not just make general elections less competitive; it also allows the locking out of challengers at the primary stage.The institutional party has gained further thanks to a July Supreme Court decision striking down the federal campaign finance prohibition on coordinated spending by parties for candidates. The anti-coordination measure prevented parties from becoming conduits for dark money. The decision likely helps the Republicans in the short term, but in the medium term bolsters both parties’ insiders at the expense of outsiders. To be sure, there is no assurance that Martin’s DNC will be able to capitalize on this new leverage this cycle: power matters only if you are competent enough to use it. But Democratic incompetency seems unlikely to endure forever.At the same time that the law is making the political landscape less competitive, a series of corporate law developments are concentrating power in the commanding heights of the data economy. According to the official story of American capitalism, a corporation with publicly traded equity is strongly responsive to its shareholders. Its original technicians took pride in how their design choices ensured that minority shareholders couldn’t be exploited by managers or controlling shareholders. At least in its own telling, corporate law diffuses concentrated power, and so enables collective choice via market discipline.Yet over the last two decades, venture capitalists in Silicon Valley have perfected corporate governance tools to circumvent even the residue of shareholder primacy. Their main instrument has been something called the dual-class share. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, the world’s largest ever initial public offering (IPO), provides an example.SpaceX’s public offering sold one kind of equity, called Class A shares, to the public. Each share gets one vote. But there are also super-voting Class B shares, with ten votes per share. As a result of his concentrated ownership of Class B shares, Musk currently owns about 40 percent of the company’s equity capital while controlling about 80 percent of the voting rights. And the company has bound itself to selling Class B shares only to Musk and Musk-related entities in the future. In effect, the dual-class structure locks in Musk’s control — and eviscerates ordinary shareholders’ power — forever.Dual-class shares aren’t the only legal trick for shoring up corporate insiders’ power. OpenAI and Anthropic alike use complex governance devices — a nonprofit holding company and a long-term trust — to much the same effect. As they follow SpaceX into the public equity markets, expect the founders of those firms to preserve near-total control of those companies. The result will be that the most important and wealthiest public companies in the United States will be under the almost total control of a small coterie of hyperwealthy founders, one that can comfortably fit in a conference room. The concentration of power over the economy will be immense.Dual-class shares aren’t new. As David Kampmann has brilliantly documented, the rise of dual-class shares started in 2004 with Google’s IPO; Facebook then followed a similar route in 2012. Their success led to a wider acceptance of a “founder control” model of corporate governance. What’s different today is the fact that dual-class firms now occupy not a niche, but the most profitable and consequential sector of the US economy.These two trends are closely connected. Contrary to some public narratives, campaign financing over the past two decades has not been the province of mainly large corporations. Rather, it has been a handful of “megadonors” — including, of course, Musk — who have increasingly dominated political spending. The durable concentrations of equity created by dual-class shares can serve as collateral for such donors, enabling them to borrow profligately for their pet political projects. This is a strategy known as “buy, borrow, die,” commonly used by the hyperrich to create liquid wealth even as they hold on to equity, then passing it on to heirs under a relatively sparing tax regime.Founders thus become political rainmakers, while their heirs retain both a firm hold on the corporate heights and the ability to translate that corporate control into political hegemony. The potential for dynastic control, over and above the forces that ensure familial transmission of wealth and privilege in the ordinary course of things, is obvious.The legal architectures of concentrated economic and political power are joined at the hip. This functional link between esoteric details of campaign finance law and corporate governance is easy to miss. Even legal scholars tend to look at these fields in isolation, missing their connections. Yet to grasp the scale and vector of contemporary reaction, it’s necessary to understand how the law matters to the Left’s political projects. Only an exacting accounting of the subtle filaments by which it joists economic and political power illuminates the stakes for what they truly are.

articles.title: The Dangerous Rise of Victimhood Nationalism
articles.author: Kap Seol
articles.content: South Korea has strong traditions of class struggle and left-wing political organization. Unfortunately, this has generally not been reflected in the development of Korean radical theory, which has tended to be heavily derivative of work published in other countries and languages. Lim Jie-hyun’s book Victimhood Nationalism is a welcome exception to this rule. Lim is a historian at Sogang University in Seoul, and his book is a genuinely original contribution from a country that has long relied on intellectual imports. It draws on case studies from Poland, Germany, Israel, Korea, and Japan to illustrate a phenomenon that is becoming increasingly familiar as its champions lay claim to a status of “hereditary victimhood.” Between Perpetrator and Victim He defines the concept of “victimhood nationalism” (not the nationalism of victims) around which the book is structured as “a narrative template to grant moral superiority and political legitimacy to a present nation.” For Lim, victimhood nationalism involves a dual process of de-historicization and over-historicization. Historical facts are cleansed of their complexity and refashioned to serve the nationalist needs of a country. Along the way, victimhood nationalism objectifies and dehumanizes the victims of past injustices. Collective memory is no longer about collective reflection: it has become a historical asset to be used in the pursuit of contemporary legitimacy and power. While Lim does not explicitly make this point, victimhood nationalism appears to be underpinned by a form of popular demand from below to forget, sanitize, or reinterpret a nation’s darker past in ways that serve present-day needs. Germany’s collective memory of the atrocities of World War II, for example, frequently lingers behind broader narratives about the universal causes of war and human violence. In Japan, meanwhile, wartime guilt is often subsumed within a discourse of absolute pacifism, blurring the distinction between perpetrator and victim. The longest film series in Japanese cinema is The Human Condition (1959), adapted from the eponymous 1958 novel and centered on the pacifist protagonist Kaji. Kaji’s insistence on moral innocence follows him through every experience from wartime prostitution to Soviet gulags. When I read the novel as a teenager in Seoul, I was struck by the dissonance between Kaji’s professed humanism and his racist condescension toward a Korean “ comfort woman ” who is infected with a sexually transmitted disease from Japanese soldiers. This contrasts with his devotion to his pale-skinned wife Michiko, which becomes the thread that sustains him all the way from the corruption of Japanese militarism to the bloodstained Manchurian front and ultimately into Soviet captivity. Drawing on the idea of victimhood nationalism, I now find it easy to see why the book and film served a need for the postwar Japanese, liberal and conservative alike. It functioned as a vehicle to reframe wartime experience in ways that emphasize Japanese innocence and pacifism. It is not that Kaji’s story does not reflect the broader experience of the Japanese masses during the war. However, it elides what is ultimately at stake, turning such sentiments into a unilateral apologia and obscuring the structural forces driving the violence. Borrowing From the Holocaust In Lim’s account, this postwar memory regime, often tinged at its margins with residual feelings of collective guilt and moral unease, underwent a significant transformation as it became enmeshed with the memory of the Holocaust. By 1963, Japanese peace activists and Holocaust survivors were already chanting “No more Hiroshima” and “No more Auschwitz” together at the annual ceremony in Poland marking the liberation of the concentration camp. One strong point of Lim’s case for victimhood nationalism lies in his observation of how the memory of the Holocaust, often understood primarily as a singular historical catastrophe inflicted upon a single ethnic group, has become a template through which nations cast their own history of suffering. This means recasting sufferings as diverse as nuclear bombardment, colonialism, and Stalinism in ways that invite comparison with the Holocaust, transforming national memories into collective narratives of victimhood. However, this project has often come at the expense of downplaying — or entirely overlooking — the agonies of real victims of these nations, from Japan’s military sex slaves to the political prisoners and detainees from other ethnic minorities who were persecuted under Adolf Hitler’s rule. Lim discusses the dialectical interplay between the globalization and nationalization of this transnational memory regime. The incorporation of a particular nation’s victimhood narrative into the global memory formation of the Holocaust helps it gain moral capital and dignity, which in turn reinforces the global narrative, as seen in the adaptation of “Never again” by Japanese peace activists. For Lim, the Holocaust has become a foundational frame of reference through which victims of historical tragedies are reinterpreted as martyrs, drawing on the way in which Israel commemorates the Holocaust. In the dominant Israeli national victimhood memory, the Israeli state was founded on the ashes of the Holocaust. The underlying logic is that if a Jewish state had predated the rise of Hitler, the Holocaust would not have occurred. Consequently, those who perished in Hitler’s gas chambers were not merely victims but martyrs. Germany and Japan In Germany, there was an effort to forge a postwar self-image that cleansed the sins of humanity by replacing the concrete realities of German wartime atrocities with vague, abstract questions such as “Why must humans wage war?” In collective memory, Lim argues, the Holocaust and other Nazi atrocities were seen as crimes committed by Hitler and his henchmen, for whom justice had been served through the Nuremberg Trials. Ordinary Germans, meanwhile, tended to view themselves as the first and last victims of Hitler and, ultimately, as victims of an unjust memory. For many Germans, the most horrifying memories stemmed from the experience of Germans who were interned in detention camps before their expulsion from Poland and Czechoslovakia. As early as 1949, West German political leaders already began to decontextualize German war crimes, with Hans-Christoph Seebohm, transport minister in the government of Konrad Adenauer, equating the suffering of German expellees with that of Holocaust victims. According to Lim, victimhood took center stage in Germany’s nationalist narrative after the end of the Cold War. He cites a 1995 survey commissioned by Der Spiegel , in which about 40 percent of respondents age sixty-four or older said the postwar expulsion of Germans from Central and Eastern Europe was a crime against humanity on a par with the Holocaust. This form of victimhood nationalism, based on the dichotomy between “a few Nazi criminals” and “most innocent Germans,” was central to reinforcing the national identity of the unified Germany under Helmut Kohl. Japan’s postwar memory culture, Lim suggests, was little different. He presents its cultural memory as a form of national victimology that defined the fifteen years of military rule between 1931 to 1945 as a historical aberration departing from an otherwise successful modernization process. This framework presented Japanese militarism as a deviation from, rather than a product of, Japan’s broader imperial development. Much of the Japanese public imagination attributed responsibility for wartime atrocities solely to amorphous entities such as “militarism” or “the system” while depicting ordinary Japanese as innocent victims of the war. This narrative recast the peoples of Japan and the Asian nations it conquered as common victims of Japanese militarism. For many Japanese, the memory of the atomic bombings supplies the dominant lens through which the war is remembered. Japan’s global identity as the only nation to have fallen victim to nuclear bombings has functioned, in Lim’s words, as a “screen memory that conceals Japan’s war crimes against Asian neighbors.” The dead and maimed of Hiroshima and Nagasaki are cast as victims of an “absolute evil.” In turn, this narrative of absolute evil gave rise to a form of absolute pacifism that condemns all wars as evil, detached from its historical context. The issue of accountability is largely absent from Japanese pacifism because it identifies no clear subject of responsibility. De-historicized and decontextualized, Japan’s dominant version of pacifism is used to condemn war and nuclear bombs while rarely holding Japan accountable for the imperialist wars that devastated its neighbors. In 1994, Kurihara Sadako, a poet who was critical of her country’s victimhood narrative, wrote the following words in a poem: If the atomic bombing was mercy so was the imperial army’s massacre of 20 thousand in Nanjing so was the Nazis’ gas chamber that massacred 6 million mercy. Victimhood and Violence Victimhood nationalism sanctifies victimhood into a collective form of martyrdom. Historical experiences are emptied of context, as certain elements are emphasized while others are marginalized. Lim refers to this as a combination of “historicization” and “de-historicization.” One of Lim’s insightful observations is that de-historicization and globalization can serve as instruments of national cohesion and obstacles to transnational solidarity. By lifting national experiences of suffering up to a globally recognized moral framework associated with Holocaust remembrance, they strengthen collective identity at home. At the same time, they obscure the suffering of colonial subjects and other victims of historic persecution, evidently limiting the possibility of a genuinely universal memory politics. The timeline of Lim’s book stops in the early twenty-first century. We are already living in a period when victimhood nationalism appears to be undergoing another transformation following an earlier phase marked by apologetic and self-pitying narratives of victimhood. Recently, we have witnessed cases in which nationalist narratives of victimhood took a violent turn in Russia, Israel, and elsewhere, with claims of historical suffering invoked to justify the infliction of violence on others in the name of “Never again.” Benjamin Netanyahu’s explicit linking of his atrocities in Palestine with the fearful memory of the Holocaust has been widely documented. Vladimir Putin’s rhetoric portraying Mother Russia as a historical victim of the West is also well known. Sooner rather than later, we may observe Japan and Germany using their own victimhood narratives to rearm themselves against China and Russia. Ahistorical narratives of nationalism are particularly corrosive. Trap of Universality In principle, the Left is internationalist, ultimately opposing all forms of nationalism even while critically defending the right of the oppressed to self-determination. For the Left, victimhood nationalism constitutes a particular challenge. While it is often articulated in universal moral languages — human rights, peace, and Holocaust remembrance — it blurs, or even glosses over, the memories of the devastation wrought by imperialism, colonialism, and authoritarian rule. Lim’s case is a warning against the political use of remembrance, and that scope can likely reach beyond his proposition of victimhood nationalism. In order for “Never again” to retain its universal meaning, the Left must remain vigilant against all forms of narratives cloaked in the language of universal victimhood.

articles.title: The Odyssey Is a Thrilling, Reactionary Lament
articles.author: Grant Morgan
articles.content: The Odyssey , Christopher Nolan’s cinematic retelling of Homer’s epic poem, has taken the country by storm. While on vacation back home in southern Illinois, I visited a Dolby theater with my family to experience it myself — and was not disappointed. The film delivered spectacular visuals, clever effects, and breathtaking sound design. Dozens of scenes had my heart racing as massive jumps in decibels shook the walls around me and the seat beneath me. When the Cyclops was stabbed in the eye, its screams of agony bounced off the walls of the cave and landed directly in our theater, creating a real sense of terror. When Circe transformed the soldiers into pigs, the sound of crunching bone leaped into each aisle and made my skin crawl. The acting was superb, as was Nolan’s ability to instill energy and suspense into a story that has been told, retold, and parodied hundreds of times. At a moment of widespread oversaturation and unoriginality, Nolan’s passionate retelling inspired and captivated. It was by no means perfect, but as a rendering of the poem’s narrative, warnings, and symbols, it excelled. I was entertained; my family was entertained; and my mother, a former mythology teacher, was so entertained that she saw it twice. Just as fascinating has been watching critics and commentators interpret the film’s message about norms and social bonds. Invoked throughout the film, “Zeus’s Law” serves as the Bronze Age’s Golden Rule, meant to instill mutual respect between individuals and society. Hospitality, tradition, and empathy are all held in high regard, with institutions and individuals alike called on to care for guests and their needs. Hosts are to be kind and courteous, as are guests; palaces are to provide moral direction and some of society’s bounty to the underclasses; and strangers and beggars are to be treated with care, since any one of them might be a god in disguise who dare not be angered. From very early in the film, it becomes clear that Nolan is critiquing our current moment from a small-‘c’ conservative perspective. The historian Bret Devereaux put this argument well in a review when he described Nolan’s understanding of Zeus’s Law and civilizational structure as almost Burkean in outlook. Nolan views civilizational collapse, in Ancient Greece and in our own period, as driven by a breakdown of morality, mercy, decorum, and social bonds. Vice — greed, hedonism, violence, sadism — becomes the new id driving human pursuits, creating a society where collective well-being is destroyed by warped individual selfishness. We see this conservative vision play out in Troy. Odysseus’s Trojan Horse at once breaks Zeus’s Law and unleashes the ungodly destruction of Troy and its people. Greek soldiers pouring through the city’s gates, with Agamemnon in command, devolve into wild, debauched creatures hell-bent on destruction. Women and children are killed, raped, and enslaved; men are slaughtered by the hundreds; sacred statues and temples are desecrated and innocent priests cut down. With social bonds and morals broken, humanity is launched into a world where anarchy, power, and brutality govern one’s relationship — or lack thereof — to society’s structures and obligations. Odysseus realizes as much in Athena’s temple. It is, after all, his own men who behead children and priestesses, who set fires that engulf homes and shops, who desecrate both gods and mortals by violating a sacred law meant to be upheld by all. Amid the jubilant celebrations and toasts, Odysseus begins to feel dread, humiliation, and trauma. He is hailed as a hero, a tactician who brought unequivocal victory to his people. But internally, his mind begins to suffer. He has broken the tenets of a Burkean social order in which obligation and moral standing come before individual interest. Who was he, just one man, to break an order that had held for untold generations? The trip through Hades — or hell — serves as a reckoning with the collapse of the traditional order. Soldiers who perished at Troy are not welcomed as heroes in the afterlife but buried under ash and torment. Veterans who made it home are not greeted as returning victors; they become beggars or thieves in a world where mercy and empathy are in steep decline. Much like the Reign of Terror that followed the French Revolution, the break with the traditions of old is presented as begetting something far more barbaric. Our inherited rights, bequeathed to us by the dead and upheld for generations through moral and cultural obligation, are abandoned and burned, leaving behind a decayed society. Cities and ports are laid to waste as the breakdown in norms, hospitality, and trade spreads anarchy and ruin. The dreaded “sea people,” really just fellow Greeks fleeing collapse and war, are said to be bringing the apocalypse. Terror is everywhere, and no rule is infallible. Nolan’s Burkean interpretation of The Odyssey , with its emphasis on traditional moral orders and social obligations, casts our present as a moment of ideological and social rupture. At the end of history, politicians devoid of decorum, respectability, and empathy turn toward a politics of cruel avarice and bitterness. We are all now the people of Ithaca, watching our social order collapse into immorality and war. Borders have been militarized against the world’s various “sea peoples”; entire swaths of the earth have been turned into zones of cruelty, violence, and inhospitality; the law has been weaponized to attack norms, individuals, and institutions and to ensure personal enrichment; international arbitration and coordination have been supplanted by a brazen imperial appetite for conquest. Whatever ideals once kept our liberal order in check now seem dead and buried, cast aside by a generation that has traded tradition and national obligation for blood, wealth, and power. The powerful vision animating Nolan’s Odyssey no doubt resonates with Americans who feel our current moment is unprecedented and devoid of reason. Walls are being erected, gates closed, and cosmopolitanism thrown to the wolves in favor of retrenchment and new forms of nationalism. Supply-Side Liberalism as Zeus’s Law For liberals especially, this Burkean interpretation ironically makes a lot of sense. After all, many of the traditions and norms we have come to cherish are vestiges of American liberalism. Mid-century liberalism delivered virtually all the laws, rulings, and norms around privacy, speech, property, and equality that have come to be viewed as fixed and permanent. Liberalism itself has become a kind of tradition. Our economic logic fits this mold too, with deregulation, tax incentives, and supply-side growth serving as cornerstones of liberalism’s modern orthodoxy. For well over fifty years, America’s social order has bequeathed a slate of rights and obligations without fundamentally breaking from the New Deal’s administrative machinery. The role of labor has of course diminished since its prominence in the 1940s, but even this was not much of a disruption. After World War II, labor and working-class militancy were gradually converted into just another interest group alongside activists, nonprofits, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and businesses. Unions still played some role in the liberal electoral coalition, but they were no longer where the party’s energy was felt. In this analogy, Zeus’s Law is our own liberal social order. Our law, put simply, was a social bond carrying certain expectations and promises toward both capitalism and the individual. Individual rights and social freedoms — privacy, abortion, contraception, freedom of religion, the de jure end of segregation — were to be protected and removed from political contention. The American dream, or the idea of social mobility more generally, was to be at least hypothetically available to all who were willing to work hard, innovate, and educate themselves in the burgeoning fields of the future. As for state and local governments, the supply-side investments and grants that for decades had flowed from federal coffers into regional business groups, communities, and projects would continue apace. Supply-siders would drive the direction of federal money, delivering an economy that was not planned but not entirely private either. From the 1970s onward, this moral and political order offered everyone a supply-side liberal contract that supposedly guaranteed the right to a safe and secure life. Departing from more communal and class-based visions, it was a new way of seeing your fellow citizens — a way of spotting a potential Zeus in every passerby. Every person was to be bequeathed a fair playing field, with government there to help business and consumer, entrepreneur and professional alike, get ahead and enjoy the bounties of individual striving and growth. Nolan witnessed this order firsthand in his childhood in the UK and the United States. Growing up in London and spending summers in Evanston, Illinois, he experienced these promises in urban centers defined by finance, real estate, tech, and above all steady growth. At the start of his career, in the 1990s and early 2000s, this bond and its obligations were at their most admired: it was an era of faith in markets, faith in limited government, and faith in the power of individuals to educate themselves, invest, and soar. Political battles, when they broke into national consciousness, never verged on outright weaponization or mass civil unrest. Government shutdowns came and went; Bush v. Gore caused controversy, but the country moved forward with the ostensible president-elect; the dot-com bubble briefly roiled markets and 401(k)s, then disappeared from the headlines. The 9/11 attacks jolted the country into patriotic fervor and sent soldiers overseas, but this wasn’t exactly new in American politics. As for stark differences between the parties, both sides of the aisle were happy to support supply-side policies, vote for the Iraq War, and drag their feet on social issues — except, of course, crime. Hard crackdowns in the legal system — broken-windows policing, three-strikes laws, harsher sentencing — ensued, as did punitive drug policies that swelled the country’s prison population. Long-standing entitlements were ended and replaced with tax credits, temporary assistance, and a growing emphasis on work requirements and individual merit. The law did little to protect working-class women, who were now expected to join the labor market, earn less than their male counterparts, and still care for their children with dwindling assistance. Nor did the safety net address the regional inequalities and diseases of despair spreading through the rusting Northeast and Midwest. Nolan’s analogy between Zeus’s Law and our own social order is appealing, especially to those who see our period as marked by a sudden collapse in norms and sanity. When the Trojan Horse is shown burning alongside Troy, it renders the viewer speechless — contemplating the film’s meaning in their own lives, in a moment when unprecedented political behavior and environmental crisis alike seem to signal divine damnation. But despite the stunning imagery and direction, Nolan’s analogy ultimately falls flat, because our current moment is one of continuation, not divergence. Put another way, Nolan sees a moral rupture that never took place. America was not blown off course by some foundational violation of contract or bond. Deregulation, market-oriented models, and attacks on labor were underway as early as the 1940s and 1950s. Brent Cebul’s Illusions of Progress makes clear just how dominant supply-side liberalism and business-friendly policies were within our order all along. It was, after all, the American West and South — bastions of conservatism and reaction — that benefited most from federal investment delivered through the mechanisms of federalism and public-private partnerships. Even in the heyday of the New Deal state, government intervention in the economy was delivered through existing channels that often bypassed entire populations and regions. Rather than relying on public institutions or state-owned assets, as in a social democratic state, the American government became the funder and insurer of the market, with a weak presence on the ground. Instead of directly building things or providing services, it worked through tax cuts, inducements, outsourcing, and subsidies. Government, business, and philanthropy became joined at the hip in a triangular system that channeled federal dollars to private organizations. The mid-century male breadwinner benefited, as did business and the ever growing nonprofit sector. This, in essence, was as far as our welfare state was willing to go. And even at its strongest, labor militancy and class consciousness were never the ideological or material underpinnings of this structure. They might have generated different political outcomes, but sadly they never did. So while stagflation and neoliberalism battered labor and remade the country’s economy from industrial to service-oriented, these events never broke us away from the triangular supply-side bond that still drives the country today. This is where Nolan’s analogy fails: We never had a sack of Troy. We never broke Zeus’s Law. And that is precisely the problem with our current moment. The Odyssey frames our moment as one in which morals and bonds have been broken. But in reality, our social order has continued unabated, with supply-side liberalism chugging along despite growing polarization, inequality, and political upheaval. Sure, social questions have grown more contentious, especially around abortion and LGBTQ rights, but just as in the 1980s and 1990s, they have never been the fulcrum of our order. Broken-windows policing disproportionately targeted working-class and African American communities, harming core constituencies of the liberal coalition. Welfare reform overwhelmingly hurt single mothers, working-class people, and the poor — all groups liberalism purported to fight for. Democrats infamously dragged their feet on gay marriage and abortion protections, only vehemently defending the latter once Roe v. Wade was overturned. Continuation, Not Aberration The core bond of supply-side liberalism — its promise of wealth, unfettered markets, and market autonomy — has yet to be broken. Donald Trump has derailed certain commitments, like free trade and the GOP’s ostensible anti-statism. But those commitments could always be shifted to protect the broader bond and its spoils. Despite historic tariffs and administrative curtailment, no paradigm-ending event has occurred. Ours is still a triangular system of big government, big business, and big philanthropy. Federal dollars still flow to states, communities, businesses, and nonprofits and still enable the basic functions of a modern state. This structure has not changed. Nolan’s suggestion seems to be that Trumpism is the cause of our rupture — that a lack of respect for decorum, institutional legitimacy, and morality has generated this crisis; that the open embrace of nationalism and cruelty is driving us toward greater inequality and violence. Crucially, we are meant to believe that we have become something fundamentally different, that we have broken from the old order and mutated away from what we used to be and stand for. Surely, the thinking goes, we were not always just imperial operators serving an American capitalism that benefits the few and disrespects everyone else. But capitalist America has always been thus. During the era of consensus, Washington bombed nation after nation and killed untold numbers of innocent people and fomented coups and civil wars to defend banana companies and financial institutions. American politicians, in thrall to the domestic capitalist class, deregulated business, privatized the welfare state, and protected elites’ right to exploitation and to untaxed wealth. At the height of neoliberal triumphalism, the United States invaded Iraq and Afghanistan, then caused a global financial crisis that pushed millions to the brink of poverty and starvation. When was the supposed rupture? Trump’s antics have been historic, but as many have argued, he is no aberration. Plenty of Republicans, especially in the base, held Trumpian beliefs well before 2016 — and those beliefs won’t suddenly dissipate when the man himself leaves office. No rupture in America’s social order has occurred. Troy has not been sacked, and Zeus’s Law has not been broken, because no fundamental part of America’s social bond has been severed. The supply-side, business-friendly state that emerged from the consolidation of the New Deal is still kicking, its fundamental logic still in place. The Odyssey is an entertaining film, but its conservative critique of American society is simply wrong. We are still living in the Bronze Age. Society has not collapsed, revolution has not occurred, and no alternative has appeared. We are living, instead, at the point in an order when purpose seems exhausted, promises weak, and the future tenuous. Much like Odysseus, we all now find ourselves adrift at sea, hoping to make our way back to a mythical, happy home that never existed in the first place.

articles.title: Trump Gets Real About US Dominance of Latin America
articles.author: Andre Pagliarini
articles.content: In 1914, addressing the University of Buenos Aires, President Theodore Roosevelt called the Monroe Doctrine a policy “which the United States promulgated, partly as a matter of policy in its own interest, partly as a matter of policy in the interest of all the republics of the New World.” Earlier this week, the State Department posted a five-minute video to its official account on Twitter tracing a straight line from James Monroe’s 1823 message to Congress through the Spanish-American War, the Roosevelt Corollary, and the Cuban Missile Crisis, arriving finally at the abduction of Nicolás Maduro from Caracas this past January. The video presents Donald Trump as the doctrine’s “latest defender.”Dispensing with two centuries of diplomatic euphemism, the video concludes that “American dominance in the Western Hemisphere will never be questioned again.” Rather than a defense of hemispheric independence that just so happens to benefit the United States, the Monroe Doctrine today is presented openly as a tool of American dominance.This is not entirely surprising — the pretense of goodwill has never been central to the MAGA project. But for most of its history, the Monroe Doctrine required a certain interpretive work to be understood as an instrument of US hegemony. Defenders could point to its origins as a warning against European recolonization, a solidaristic shield extended over shaky, newly independent republics. Critics had to trace how the shield became a cudgel.Henry M. Brackenridge, who led a special mission to Brazil in 1817 at President James Monroe’s behest, captured the ambiguous sensibility of US officials. “As an American, I cannot but feel a kind of pride in looking forward to the lofty destinies of this new world,” he wrote, concluding, however, that “when we consider the vast capacities and resources of Brazil, it is not visionary to say, that this empire is destined to be our rival.” All suspicion and no grace or gesture at understanding, the Trump administration is clearly being moved by the darkest historical impulses of the United States toward Latin America.On the day after the State Department tweet, Celso Amorim — chief foreign policy adviser to Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and former foreign minister of Latin America’s largest nation — told Brazil’s Congress that the video calls into question the sovereignty of every country in Latin America. He noted that Brazil goes unmentioned but insisted this hardly matters. A declaration of hemispheric dominance does not need to name targets if it claims them all.Amorim then told lawmakers what enforcement could look like. Washington’s recent designation of Brazilian criminal factions as terrorist organizations, he warned, cannot be read apart from this context. Elastic interpretations of the terrorist and narcoterrorist labels have already justified military operations elsewhere.Ironically, the government of Dom Pedro I was the first in South America to publicly endorse the Monroe Doctrine. The young emperor had the US president’s declaration printed in Portuguese and circulated as welcome news. Brazil, which had earned its independence only two years prior and remained anxious to assert itself in the region and beyond, read the doctrine as a promise that the New World would be left to govern itself. José Silvestre Rebello, Brazil’s first envoy to Washington, invoked exactly this logic when he pressed John Quincy Adams for recognition, which came on May 26, 1824, following the adoption of Brazil’s first constitution. Brazil’s independence was just and constitutional, Rebello argued, and Brazil should therefore be free to follow its own path.That was the bargain as the most optimistic nineteenth-century Latin Americans understood it. The hemisphere would be closed to European empire, and the American nations would determine their own destinies. What the region got instead is well documented. Theodore Roosevelt’s 1904 corollary converted a warning to Europe into a license for the United States to police its neighbors. The doctrine underwrote occupations in the Caribbean and Central America, gunboat diplomacy, dollar diplomacy, and, during the Cold War, support for coups and dictatorships from Guatemala to Chile to Brazil itself.Rep. Delia Ramirez, whose parents fled Guatemala during the US-backed slaughter there, responded to the State Department’s video by calling it cheap imperialist propaganda for an approach that has delivered “instability, deep poverty, extreme migration, and colonialism throughout Latin America and the Caribbean.”Last November, the administration’s National Security Strategy announced a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, declaring that the United States would deny non-hemispheric competitors — above all China — any foothold in the Americas and treat the region’s strategic assets as matters of American security. The first months of 2026 showed what that means in practice. Maduro was seized in a US military operation the administration called Operation Absolute Resolve. Cuba, meanwhile, has been subjected to an expanding sanctions regime.“What we’re trying to teach them is there are no escape valves,” Rubio told Axios.In a recent interview, Amorim called the Venezuela operation a violation of international law in its oldest sense, the law of nations, and observed that its only recent parallel is the fate of Saddam Hussein. He was careful to say he was not defending Maduro. That is precisely the point. One need not defend any particular government to grasp that a world in which Washington abducts hemispheric heads of state is a world in which no government’s sovereignty is secure.With the bilateral relationship at its lowest point in decades — perhaps its historical nadir — Brazil has particular reasons to fret about the implications of this message from Washington. Brazil has never sought a break from the United States. It endorsed the Monroe Doctrine before any of its neighbors. It has fought alongside the United States, traded with it, and cooperated with administrations of both parties. What Brazil has sought, consistently, is something more valuable and apparently harder to grant than friendship: recognition of its right to pursue its own interests as Brazilians define them, even when doing so inconveniences Washington.Lula trades with China because China buys what Brazil sells. He talks to Moscow and Tehran because Brazil believes conflict ends through mediation rather than escalation. Despite the Trump administration’s implications, none of this constitutes alignment with US enemies. It constitutes the foreign policy of a large, self-governing nation that declines to live inside anyone’s sphere of influence.That refusal is the real target of the video. Amorim has argued that multipolarity is degenerating into something cruder: a carve-up of the world into spheres of influence, with the great powers rhetorically condemning one another’s land grabs while respecting them in practice. Asked what Brazil would do if the United States invaded, Brazil’s defense minister said recently that a helpless Brazil “would have to open the gate.” For his part, Amorim has concluded that Brazil cannot match the military power of the United States, China, or Russia, and should not try, but it can make aggression costly. Hence his call for defense spending approaching 2 percent of GDP and for a national strategy around critical minerals, where Brazil already ranks second in the world in rare earth mineral reserves. A country announces that hemispheric dominance is its birthright; its largest neighbors start pricing submarines. This is how the Trump administration has the hemisphere thinking.The deeper problem is the one many Latin Americans identified in 1823. A doctrine that closes the hemisphere to outside empires is only as good as the self-restraint of the power announcing it. Simón Bolívar realized this early on. Brazilian diplomats saw it by the 1820s, when Rebello, no republican, left Washington convinced that the United States favored its own interests over any abstract principle.The doctrine’s defenders have always insisted that it protects the Americas. Its history shows something narrower: it protects American primacy. The State Department’s video has now discarded the distinction. The United States has stopped pretending that the Monroe Doctrine was about anything other than its own freedom of action. Latin America clocked this two centuries ago. Washington is only now catching up with its own record.Brazilians will go to the polls in October under the shadow of capricious tariffs imposed for political gain, terrorist designations that could license intervention, and a superpower openly proclaiming dominance over their hemisphere. If they conclude that sovereignty is on the ballot, they will be reading the moment correctly.

articles.title: AES countries rebuke Nigerian president after he blamed Sahel states for insecurity
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: The Alliance of Sahel States (AES) has condemned Nigerian President Bola Tinubu for fueling “frustrations between peoples bound by history, geography, and fraternity.”​ The bloc comprising Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger summoned the Nigerian Chargé d’Affaires to a meeting in Burkina Faso’s capital, Ouagadougou, on August 6, to protest against Tinubu’s blaming the three Sahelian countries for Nigeria’s security woes. Read more: Nigerian government losing ground to a resurgent Boko Haram and its IS-affiliated splinter Multiple security crises plague Nigeria: Boko Haram ravaging the north, bandit attacks in the northwest, and communal violence in the central region driven by a contest for land between farmers and herders.​ This violence is both exacerbating the worsening hunger and cost of living crisis triggered by Tinubu’s ruthless implementation of the IMF-prescribed neoliberal restructuring. The economic crisis is, in turn, fueling the violence. Read more: World Bank acknowledges poverty increase in Nigeria, but doubles down on the reforms causing it In this backdrop, addressing the traditional leaders on July 30, Bola Tinubu sought to deflect responsibility, saying, “Some of them (the terrorists) are not Nigerian. You see, the problem of insecurity in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger only exacerbates our difficulties.”​ All three countries have emerged out of mass protests amid which the regimes propped up by their former colonizer France were ousted in popularly supported coups, leading to the formation of military governments that went on to expel French troops.​ This toppling of French-backed governments began first in Mali in 2020, followed by Burkina Faso in 2022. France, whose troops were already expelled from the two countries by then, initially refused to back down and threatened war when its regime fell in Niger later in 2023, fronting the remaining countries in its neocolonial bloc, the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), to invade Niger. ​ Tinubu, the chairperson of ECOWAS at the time, was keen on sending the Nigerian military – struggling to provide security within the country – to invade its neighbor to restore the ousted regime for France. However, the Nigerian parliament refused to authorize the military operation.​ Read more: Nigeria’s Senate refuses to support ECOWAS plan for West-backed military intervention On the other side, Mali and Burkina Faso came to Niger’s defense, and the three formed a military pact that has since evolved into a political and economic bloc, the AES.​ Pursuing a drastically different economic policy to the one Tinubu is implementing in Nigeria, the AES countries have expanded the public sector and exerted greater control over their mineral wealth. Their economic advances in industry and agriculture have been widely acknowledged, including in the business press. Read more: Burkina Faso expands budget as mining reforms boost state revenues Despite registering high economic growth, the countries are fraught with insecurity, coming under frequent large-scale attacks by a coalition of Al-Qaeda-affiliated JNIM and the Tuareg separatist rebel group, the FLA. The AES maintains these groups are proxy forces used by France to derail their advancement toward sovereignty.​ Read more: Mali fights yet another wave of attacks on multiple cities by terror groups ​ However, even before these large-scale attacks began across the three countries, Niger was already coming under attack from Boko Haram, originating in Nigeria.​ Reminding the Nigerian Chargé d’Affaires of this at the meeting in Ouagadougou on August 6, Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister Karamoko Jean Marie Traore complained that Tinubu’s remarks demonstrate “a contempt for the sacrifice made by the Nigerien army against Boko Haram for years.”​ Nigeria’s diplomat reportedly acknowledged the AES role in combating terrorism – specifically the role of Niger in stopping attacks targeting Nigeria.​ “We are paying the price, but the real enemies are elsewhere,” added Traore. “We would have preferred a more accurate presentation of the security situation [by Tinubu], rather than placing the blame for a complex situation on neighboring countries, at the risk of fueling misunderstandings and frustrations between peoples bound by history, geography, and fraternity.”​ The Nigerian diplomat assured that he would take their note of protest to the capital, Abuja. Traore assured him that instead of condemning Nigeria for their insecurity, the AES countries chose to engage with the neighbor, insisting that they are in a “joint and shared fight.”

articles.title: The International Monetary Fund’s Africa policy is underdevelopment
articles.author: Grieve Chelwa
articles.content: Across Africa, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) presents itself as the custodian of macroeconomic stability. Its latest Article IV staff reports on Ethiopia . Malawi , Nigeria , South Africa , and Zambia are written for economies with very different histories and institutions. Yet they converge on a familiar prescription: fiscal consolidation, tighter monetary policy, market-determined exchange rates, subsidy reform, deregulation and “private-sector-led growth.” No serious economist can dismiss macroeconomic stability. High inflation destroys wages, foreign-exchange shortages choke production, and out-of-control debt eventually forces adjustment. But stability is a means, not a development strategy. Read together, these five reports expose the central weakness of the Fund’s approach in Africa: it is much clearer about how the state should retreat than about how African economies will acquire the productive capabilities needed to grow, diversify, and create decent jobs. Article IV consultations are formally surveillance rather than loan agreements, and not every recommendation is a binding condition. But the distinction is less reassuring than it sounds. Zambia and Ethiopia are already under Fund programs; Malawi’s program expired without a review; and in Nigeria and South Africa the Fund’s assessment influences credit ratings, investors, and the terms on which governments can borrow. These reports therefore define the boundaries of what international finance considers “sound” policy, even when the Fund supplies no money directly. The country details are revealing. In Malawi , the Fund calls for urgent stabilization to move from aid dependence to a private-sector-led economy. It stresses fiscal and monetary tightening, exchange-rate adjustment and the removal of administrative obstacles. Yet Malawi’s private economy consists overwhelmingly of small farmers and informal firms facing expensive credit, unreliable infrastructure, and scarce foreign exchange. Calling for the private sector to lead does not conjure into existence firms capable of industrial investment. In Zambia , fiscal consolidation, fuel-subsidy reform, and debt restructuring sit alongside hopes for more mining investment, public-private partnerships and competition. The report itself notes that bank lending rates averaged more than 26% in early 2025 and that private credit was below half the sub-Saharan African average. Under those conditions, which Zambian manufacturer can compete with a multinational mining company that raises finance abroad? The Ethiopia report is more explicit about transitioning from public- to private-sector-led growth. It endorses exchange-rate liberalization, reduced financial repression, greater foreign investment, and the possible privatization of commercially oriented state enterprises. But Ethiopia’s previous development model, for all its faults, used public investment and directed credit to build infrastructure and productive capacity. Dismantling those instruments before strong domestic firms and development-finance alternatives exist risks replacing state leadership not with competitive Ethiopian capitalism, but with foreign ownership of the most profitable assets. For South Africa , the Fund declares that the state-led model has reached its limits and describes private-sector-driven growth as the “only viable option.” It recommends greater private participation in electricity and logistics, product-market liberalization, and more flexible labor markets. South Africa has a more developed domestic capitalist class than most African economies. Even there, however, ownership and finance remain highly concentrated, while mass unemployment weakens domestic demand. The issue is not simply state versus market, but which institutions direct investment, towards what sectors, and under whose ownership. In Nigeria , the Fund praises fuel-subsidy removal, an end to monetary financing and foreign-exchange reform for restoring investor confidence. In the same breath, it acknowledges that poverty and food insecurity have risen. Credit is concentrated in oil and gas, with virtually no new lending to small firms and households. This is the contradiction in miniature: improved indicators for international investors are treated as progress even when productive domestic investment and household welfare remain depressed. Throughout these reports, “the private sector” is presented as a single actor. It is not. Africa has millions of traders, farmers and small firms, but in many countries only a thin domestic class of firms with the capital, technology, and organizational capacity to invest at scale. The investor positioned to benefit from privatization, liberalization, mining concessions, and public-private partnerships is therefore often the multinational corporation, not an emergent national industrialist. This matters because multinational investment can generate exports while remaining an enclave: importing machinery, expatriating profits, minimizing taxes and establishing few links with domestic suppliers. Foreign investment can contribute to development, but only when disciplined by local-content rules, technology-transfer requirements, strategic procurement and institutions that nurture domestic firms. The IMF’s framework treats these industrial-policy tools principally as distortions rather than as mechanisms through which today’s rich and industrializing countries built productive capacity. Even the Fund’s own research identifies an additional constraint. A 2025 IMF working paper estimates that sub-Saharan African sovereigns pay an extra 46 basis points on Eurobond issuance after controlling for credit rating, maturity, currency and global conditions. During global shocks, this “African premium” exceeds 120 basis points. African states are thus urged to withdraw precisely because borrowing is unusually expensive, while weak public investment makes their economies less productive and keeps risk perceptions high. This is a vicious circle, not a route to transformation. Kevin Gallagher and Njūgūna Ndūng’ū recently argued that the Fund remains caught in an austerity trap : programs regularly underperform their growth forecasts, underestimate fiscal multipliers, and fail to transform the export structures that cause balance-of-payments crises. Their proposed alternative, country-specific, countercyclical programs centered on growth and redistribution, should inform the Fund’s current review of program design and conditionality. Africa does not need indifference to inflation or debt. It needs a different sequencing of adjustment. Protect public investment and universal services; restructure debt earlier and more deeply; tax mineral rents, wealth, and illicit financial flows; expand concessional finance; rebuild development banks; and use industrial policy to create domestic firms capable of learning, exporting, and employing people. Social-spending floors should be binding, not decorative, and adjustment should be measured against employment, poverty and productive investment as well as fiscal balances. The relevant choice is not between an inefficient state and an idealized market. It is between an economic settlement that reproduces commodity dependence and foreign corporate dominance, and one that builds African productive power through an industrial policy, a monetary policy, and continental thinking. Until the IMF confronts that choice, its programs may stabilize balance sheets on behalf of the external creditors while leaving the structures that generate crises for the people firmly intact. The IMF policy for Africa is to develop underdevelopment. Grieve Chelwa (Senior Fellow, Tricontinental and Associate Professor of Political Economy at the Africa Institute) and Vijay Prashad (Director, Tricontinental) are the authors of the recently published How the International Monetary Fund Stranges Africa (Johannesburg: Inkani Books, 2026). Chelwa is on the Papal Commission on Debt and Development in the Global South. This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz will remain shut, says Iran, as US threatens intensified economic warfare
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Iran rejected fresh US threats about an indefinite naval blockade and other tactics of economic warfare over the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, August 13, calling them a bigger miscalculation than the joint US-Israeli war launched against the country in February. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reacted to threats made by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that his country can keep the naval blockade on Iran indefinitely. He warned the Donald Trump administration against being yet again deceived by “fake intelligence.” Iran also rejected successive claims made by Trump and his energy secretary, Chris Wright, about the control over the Strait of Hormuz and the normalization of oil exports through it. “The US has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I think we will keep it,” Trump had said in a social media post on Wednesday. Wright has repeatedly claimed that energy supplies from the Persian Gulf region have almost returned to pre-war levels. He made the claims again on Thursday claiming if one combines the energy traffic through the sea with the traffic through upgraded land infrastructure the volume of oil exports from the region would reach around 15 million barrels per day. According to various calculations, the pre-war oil export from the region was around 18.7 million barrels per day. Iran dismissed US claims, with Ali Ozamaei, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy claiming on Thursday that “the strait is closed, and reality must be seen in the field, not in the statements and remarks of US officials,” Press TV reported on Friday. Earlier, the IRGC central command had called claims of US control over the strait “nothing but fabricated lies and falsehood” and “a reflection of US army’s desperation, and helplessness.” Various independent sources have also questioned Wright’s claims about 9 million barrels of oil leaving the region through the strait alone and the rest through new land routes, calling these claims a massive exaggeration of the reality. Trump’s misinformation campaign Iran has accused Trump and other US officials of “disseminating misinformation” related to the volume of oil leaving though the strait in order to stop oil prices from rising further before the US mid-term elections. Analysts also argue that statements about the normalization of the energy trade and claims about control over the strait is part of the Trump administration’s attempts to declare victory in the war which otherwise is seen to have gone completely in the opposite direction. According to data released by trade analytics platform Kpler, only eight ships transited through the strait on Tuesday, five on Wednesday, and nine on Thursday. This is even below August’s average of 12. Around 130–140 ships used to transit from the Strait of Hormuz before the beginning of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February, which supplied for around a quarter of the world’s energy needs. Tensions are now also rising in the Bab-al-Mandab and the Red Sea, which has been used as an alternative route to export Saudi oil after the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz, global oil supplies are expected to be affected yet again. This may push the prices upward. Iran has defied US pressure, strikes, and intensified economic warfare, and refused to lift its restrictions on the traffic through the strait, claiming it would only be normalized if the war against it ends and other conditions met such as the withdrawal of sanctions, lifting of the naval blockade and release of all its frozen assets overseas. This would remain the case irrespective of the fate of its ongoing talks with Oman to devise a common mechanism to manage the traffic through it, Iran has said. Meanwhile, Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, issued fresh threats of intensified economic warfare against Iran in the coming days. “We are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country” Bessent said during an interview on Thursday claiming “it will be a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports.”
